title: Traversing with Pointers
concept: Instead of an index (i), you can move a pointer (p) to traverse an array

steps.title: Include header
steps.explanation:
`#include <stdio.h>` provides access to output functions.

This lesson covers the pattern of traversing an array using pointer movement (`p++`) instead of an index.

steps.title: Start of main function
steps.explanation:
After creating the main frame, the array and pointer are prepared.

Next, `p` will be moved one slot at a time to read values.

steps.title: Array declaration
steps.explanation:
The `-1` at the end of `arr` is a sentinel value that signals the end of traversal.

Using a sentinel lets you determine the end without needing a separate length variable.

steps.title: Pointer initialization
steps.explanation:
`p = arr` makes `p` point to the first element.

Now in the loop, we can read `*p` and move to the next element with `p++`.

steps.title: Condition check: *p is 10 (not -1)
steps.explanation:
`*p` is 10, which is not `-1`, so the loop body executes.

The pointer starts at `arr[0]` (address `0x1000`).

steps.title: Iteration 1: Print *p (10)
steps.explanation:
`*p` dereferences the pointer to read the value at `0x1000`, which is `10`.

The pointer reads the value without modifying the array.

steps.title: Iteration 1: p++ moves to next element
steps.explanation:
`p++` advances the pointer by `sizeof(int)` (4 bytes): `0x1000` -> `0x1004`.

Now `p` points to `arr[1]` which holds `20`.

steps.title: Condition check: *p is 20 (not -1)
steps.explanation:
`*p` is now `20`, so the loop continues.

Each iteration: check condition -> print -> advance pointer.

steps.title: Iteration 2: Print *p (20)
steps.explanation: Prints the value at `0x1004`, which is `20`.

steps.title: Iteration 2: p++ moves to next element
steps.explanation:
`p++` advances from `0x1004` to `0x1008`.

Now `p` points to `arr[2]` which holds `30`.

steps.title: Condition check: *p is 30 (not -1)
steps.explanation: `*p` is `30`, so the loop continues for one more iteration.

steps.title: Iteration 3: Print *p (30)
steps.explanation: Prints the value at `0x1008`, which is `30`. This is the last valid element.

steps.title: Iteration 3: p++ moves past last element
steps.explanation:
`p++` advances from `0x1008` to `0x100c`.

Now `p` points to `arr[3]` which holds the sentinel value `-1`.

steps.title: Loop exits: *p is -1 (sentinel found)
steps.explanation:
`*p` is now `-1`, so `*p != -1` is false and the loop terminates.

The sentinel value successfully stopped the traversal at the right point.

steps.title: Program exit
steps.explanation:
`return 0;` terminates the program.

The key pattern: read (`*p`) + move (`p++`) + sentinel termination condition.

quiz.question: What should you watch out for when traversing an array with a pointer p?
options: It's slower than using an index
There's a risk of going out of bounds
quiz.explanation:
Pointers have no brakes.
If you get the termination condition wrong (reaching `length` or `NULL` character), it keeps reading past the end of the array, causing memory errors.

misconceptions.wrong: Modern compilers make pointer traversal (p++) much faster than indexing (arr[i])
misconceptions.correct: That used to be true, but nowadays compiler optimizations make them about the same.
misconceptions.why:
For readability, using indexing (`arr[i]`) is often the better choice.
There's no need to force pointer usage.

keyTakeaway: Traversing an array with `p++` is a classic C pattern. But beware of the cliff (out-of-bounds access).
